Wiggle the toes to keep blood moving, and warm chilled feet against another person or dry insulation. Attentive foot care prevents frostbite, chilblains, and trench foot in the cold.

title: Overview of heat illness
text: Heat illness occurs when the body cannot shed enough heat to keep its core temperature safe, and it ranges in severity. Milder forms include heat cramps and heat exhaustion, while heatstroke is a life-threatening emergency. Contributing factors include high temperature, humidity, exertion, dehydration, and lack of acclimatisation. Recognising the early signs and acting promptly by cooling and resting can prevent progression to dangerous stages.

title: Heat cramps
text: Heat cramps are painful muscle spasms, often in the legs, arms, or abdomen, that can occur during or after heavy exertion in the heat, linked to sweating and loss of fluid and salts. They are an early warning that the body is under heat stress. Rest in a cool place, gently stretch the affected muscles, and rehydrate, ideally with fluids containing electrolytes, before resuming any strenuous activity.

title: Heat exhaustion
text: Heat exhaustion results from losing too much fluid and salt through sweating, with signs including heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea, a fast weak pulse, and cool clammy skin. It is a serious warning that can progress to heatstroke if ignored. Move the person to shade or a cool place, have them rest and rehydrate slowly, loosen clothing, and cool the skin. Seek help if they do not improve.

title: Heatstroke is an emergency
text: Heatstroke is a medical emergency in which the body's temperature regulation fails and the core temperature climbs to dangerous levels. Signs include hot skin, a very high temperature, confusion, altered behaviour, seizures, or loss of consciousness, and sweating may or may not be present. Call for emergency help immediately and begin aggressive cooling at once, because delay can be fatal or cause lasting organ damage.

title: Cooling a heatstroke casualty
text: While awaiting emergency help for a suspected heatstroke, move the person into shade, remove excess clothing, and cool them as fast as possible. Douse or spray with water and fan them, apply cool wet cloths or ice packs to the neck, armpits, and groin, or immerse in cool water if safe. Monitor them continuously and be ready to give first aid if they lose consciousness. Rapid cooling saves lives.

title: Seek shade in heat
text: Staying in shade dramatically reduces heat gain from direct sun, which can raise the effective temperature and burden on the body considerably. Use natural shade from trees, rocks, or terrain, or create shade with a tarp, poncho, or improvised cover, keeping a gap for air to circulate beneath it. Reducing sun exposure is one of the simplest and most effective ways to avoid heat illness in hot conditions.

title: Rest during midday heat
text: The sun and air temperature are usually most intense in the middle of the day, so scheduling rest during those hours and being active in the cooler morning and evening reduces heat stress. In hot climates and deserts, travelling at dawn, dusk, or night while resting in shade at midday conserves water and energy. Avoid strenuous effort when the heat is at its peak whenever possible.

title: Light loose clothing
text: In heat, light-coloured, loose-fitting clothing helps the body stay cooler by reflecting some sunlight and allowing air to circulate and sweat to evaporate. Loose weaves promote airflow while still shading the skin from direct sun. Although it seems logical to wear little, covering the skin with light fabric can protect against sunburn and reduce fluid loss, particularly in strong sun and desert conditions.

title: Covering skin in the desert
text: In desert heat, covering exposed skin with light, breathable clothing and shading the head and neck reduces sunburn, slows sweat evaporation losses, and lowers direct radiant heating. A wide-brimmed hat or a cloth covering the head and neck offers valuable protection. Many desert peoples traditionally wear loose, full-coverage garments for exactly these reasons, keeping the body shaded while allowing some air movement.

title: Drink regularly in heat
text: In hot conditions the body loses large amounts of water through sweat, so drink regularly rather than waiting until you feel very thirsty, since thirst lags behind actual need. Sip fluids steadily throughout the day, increase intake with exertion and heat, and monitor urine colour as a rough guide, aiming for pale rather than dark. Consistent hydration is central to preventing heat illness.

title: Electrolytes and heavy sweating
text: Prolonged heavy sweating removes salts as well as water, and replacing only water can in extreme cases dilute the body's sodium dangerously. When sweating heavily for long periods, replace electrolytes through food, oral rehydration solutions, or sports drinks alongside water. For most short activities, ordinary water and normal salty food are sufficient, but sustained exertion in heat calls for attention to salt balance.

title: Avoid overexertion in heat
text: Working or moving hard in the heat produces internal body heat on top of the environmental load, raising the risk of heat exhaustion and heatstroke. Pace yourself, take frequent rests in the shade, and reduce your workload during the hottest hours. Building in recovery breaks, sharing tasks, and postponing heavy effort until it is cooler all help keep the body's temperature within safe limits.

title: Wetting clothing to cool
text: Wetting clothing, a hat, or a cloth around the neck can help cool the body as the water evaporates and carries heat away. This is most effective in dry air where evaporation is rapid, and less so in high humidity. Use water that can be spared for this only when hydration needs are met, and combine it with shade and airflow. Damp clothing over the head and neck offers noticeable relief in dry heat.

title: Acclimatising to heat
text: The body adapts to heat over one to two weeks of gradual exposure, sweating earlier and more efficiently and conserving salt better, which improves tolerance and comfort. Newcomers to a hot climate are at higher risk of heat illness until they acclimatise. Build up activity gradually, stay well hydrated, and avoid maximal exertion in the first days, allowing the body time to adjust to the conditions.

title: Early heat illness signs
text: Recognising heat illness early allows you to act before it becomes serious. Warning signs include headache, dizziness, unusual fatigue, muscle cramps, nausea, heavy sweating, and irritability or confusion. Treat these as a signal to stop, move to shade, rest, cool the body, and rehydrate. Ignoring early symptoms and pushing on is how manageable heat stress escalates into dangerous heat exhaustion or heatstroke.

title: Danger of hot enclosed spaces
text: Temperatures inside vehicles and small enclosed spaces can rise to lethal levels within minutes on a warm day, far exceeding the outside air, even with windows cracked. Never leave people or animals in a parked vehicle in the heat. Enclosed spaces such as tents and metal structures also trap heat and can become dangerously hot, so ventilate them and avoid sheltering inside them during the day's peak.

title: Humidity and cooling
text: The body sheds heat largely by evaporating sweat, and high humidity slows that evaporation, making it harder to cool down even when the air temperature is not extreme. In humid heat, sweat drips without cooling effectively, so the risk of heat illness rises. Reduce exertion, seek airflow and shade, and be especially cautious with exercise in hot, humid conditions where the body's main cooling method is impaired.

title: Resting and recovery in heat
text: When heat stress appears, stopping to rest in a cool, shaded, and ventilated spot allows the body to shed accumulated heat and recover. Lie down, loosen clothing, elevate the legs if feeling faint, and rehydrate gradually. Do not resume strenuous activity until symptoms have fully resolved. Adequate rest breaks throughout a hot day are a preventive measure, not just a response to feeling unwell.

title: Water discipline in the desert
text: In hot, arid environments, water is the limiting resource, so plan and ration your activity around it rather than rationing water itself when you have it. Drink to meet your needs, travel in the cool hours, rest in shade during the heat, and minimise sweating through pacing and clothing. Trying to save water by not drinking while working in the heat invites dangerous heat illness and impaired judgement.

title: Sunburn and heat
text: Sunburn is skin damage from ultraviolet radiation and also reduces the skin's ability to cool the body and worsens dehydration. Protect skin with clothing, a wide-brimmed hat, and shade, and cover the back of the neck. Severe sunburn can cause blistering, fever, and illness. Preventing burns supports overall heat tolerance, so cover up during the strongest sun and reduce direct exposure during midday hours.

title: Ventilation to stay cool
text: Airflow across the skin aids cooling by carrying away heat and speeding the evaporation of sweat. Seek breezes, orient a shelter to catch moving air, and create shade that still allows air to circulate underneath rather than trapping hot, still air. In calm conditions, fanning yourself or a resting casualty can meaningfully assist cooling, especially when combined with wetting the skin in dry heat.

title: Choosing a cool rest spot
text: When resting in the heat, choose the coolest available microclimate: deep shade, higher ground catching a breeze, the shaded side of rocks or terrain, or near cooler ground and water where safe. Avoid low, still hollows that trap hot air, and avoid dark surfaces that radiate heat. A little effort to find a genuinely cool, ventilated resting place greatly improves recovery and comfort in hot conditions.

title: Timing travel in hot climates
text: In very hot regions, the safest travel strategy is often to move during the cooler parts of the day, the early morning, late evening, and sometimes at night if terrain and light allow, while resting in shade through the fierce midday heat. This reduces water loss and heat stress. Night travel carries its own hazards of navigation and footing, so weigh the trade-offs against the danger of daytime heat.

title: Heat vulnerability in people
text: Some people are more vulnerable to heat illness, including young children, older adults, those who are unwell, taking certain medications, or unaccustomed to the heat, and anyone exerting hard in hot conditions. These individuals may overheat faster and show symptoms sooner. Take extra care to keep them cool, shaded, and hydrated, and watch them closely for early signs during hot weather or activity.

title: Rehydrating safely
text: Rehydrate steadily with small, frequent amounts of fluid rather than gulping large volumes at once, which can cause nausea. Cool water is well absorbed, and for heavy or prolonged sweating, including some salts through food or an oral rehydration solution helps. Avoid very cold drinks in large amounts if they cause cramps, and never rely on caffeine or alcohol, which do not replace lost fluids effectively.

title: Shade structures in the open
text: Where natural shade is scarce, a raised cover such as a tarp, poncho, or blanket creates life-saving shade in open, hot terrain. Leaving an air gap between the cover and the ground, and ideally a double layer, keeps the space beneath cooler by letting hot air escape. Orient and anchor the shade against sun and wind, and combine it with rest to sharply reduce heat load during the hottest hours.

title: Physical work and heat load
text: Any physical work generates internal heat that adds to the environmental heat load, so in hot conditions plan tasks for cooler times, break them into shorter bouts, and rest often in the shade. Reduce the pace, share heavy jobs, and drink between efforts. Recognising that your own exertion is a major heat source helps you moderate activity before heat stress builds to dangerous levels.

title: Cooling pulse points
text: Applying cool, wet cloths or ice packs to areas where large blood vessels run near the surface, such as the neck, armpits, wrists, and groin, helps cool the body more effectively by chilling the blood that flows through them. This technique is useful when treating heat exhaustion or heatstroke alongside shade, rest, and rehydration. Combine it with fanning and wetting the skin to speed heat loss.

title: Heat and impaired judgement
text: As the body overheats, mental function declines before many people realise it, causing poor decisions, irritability, confusion, and reduced awareness of danger. This makes heat illness self-reinforcing, since an affected person may push on rather than rest. In groups, watch companions for uncharacteristic behaviour or muddled thinking in the heat, and treat it as a serious early warning that demands cooling and rest.

title: Preparing for hot conditions
text: Preparing for heat reduces risk: carry enough water and a means to shade yourself, wear light, loose, covering clothing and a hat, and plan activity around the cooler hours. Check the forecast, build in rest and water stops, and acclimatise gradually if you are new to the heat. Sensible preparation and pacing prevent most heat illness, which is far easier to avoid than to treat once it takes hold.

title: Sun rises east sets west
text: The sun rises in the general direction of east and sets in the general direction of west, giving a rough sense of direction at the start and end of the day. The exact rising and setting points shift north or south with the seasons and latitude, so this is only an approximation. Still, knowing that morning sun lies roughly east and evening sun roughly west is a useful basic reference.

title: Midday sun direction
text: At local midday the sun reaches its highest point in the sky, and its position indicates direction: in the Northern Hemisphere the midday sun lies toward the south, while in the Southern Hemisphere it lies toward the north. Near the equator it passes nearly overhead and is less useful. The shortest shadow of the day points along the north-south line, giving a reliable directional cue.

title: Shadow-stick method
text: The shadow-stick method finds direction using the sun. Push a straight stick upright into level ground and mark the tip of its shadow. Wait roughly fifteen minutes or more and mark the new shadow tip. A line joining the two marks runs roughly east-west, with the first mark toward the west and the second toward the east. A line square to it gives north-south, useful when no compass is available.

title: Shadow stick and time
text: Beyond direction, a shadow stick can give a rough sense of time. Once you establish the north-south line from the shadow's shortest length, the moment the shadow is shortest marks local midday, with the sun at its highest. Shadows lengthen and swing through the morning and afternoon, so their direction and length offer an approximate clock. This is an estimate, not a precise timekeeping method.

title: Finding Polaris
text: In the Northern Hemisphere, Polaris, the North Star, sits almost directly above the North Pole, so facing it means facing roughly north. Locate it using the Big Dipper, also called the Plough: the two stars forming the outer edge of its bowl are the pointer stars. Follow the line they make outward about five times the gap between them to reach Polaris, a moderately bright but not dazzling star.

title: Polaris marks north
text: Polaris is valuable for night navigation because, unlike other stars, it barely moves across the sky as the Earth rotates, staying fixed near true north throughout the night and across the seasons. Dropping a vertical line from Polaris straight down to the horizon marks the northerly direction on the ground. Because it points to true north, not magnetic north, it needs no correction for declination.

title: Polaris and latitude
text: The angle of Polaris above the horizon roughly equals your latitude in the Northern Hemisphere. At the North Pole it sits overhead at about ninety degrees, while near the equator it lies close to the horizon and eventually drops out of sight. Estimating its height above the horizon therefore gives an approximate latitude, a technique historically used by navigators together with simple angle-measuring tools.

title: Using the Southern Cross
text: In the Southern Hemisphere there is no bright pole star, so the Southern Cross constellation helps locate south. Identify the compact cross shape and its long axis, then extend that axis about four and a half times its length to reach an imaginary point in the sky. Dropping a line from that point straight down to the horizon indicates south. Nearby pointer stars help confirm the true cross.

title: Confirming the Southern Cross
text: Several star groups resemble the Southern Cross, so confirm the real one before navigating by it. The true Southern Cross is compact, and two bright pointer stars lie nearby along one side. Extending its long axis to find the southern point, then cross-checking with the pointers, reduces the chance of using a false cross. As with all star methods, a rough south is enough to steer by, not an exact bearing.

title: Crescent moon direction hint
text: A rough directional hint comes from a crescent moon: imagine a line through the two tips, or horns, of the crescent and extend it down to the horizon. In the tropics especially, the point where that line meets the horizon lies roughly toward the south in the Northern Hemisphere and roughly north in the Southern Hemisphere. This is only approximate and works best when the moon is well clear of the horizon.

title: Watch as a compass
text: An analogue watch set to true local time can give an approximate direction. In the Northern Hemisphere, point the hour hand at the sun; the direction halfway between the hour hand and the twelve marks roughly south. In the Southern Hemisphere, point the twelve at the sun and bisect the angle to the hour hand to find roughly north. Daylight saving and time-zone offsets reduce its accuracy.

title: The moss myth
text: The common belief that moss always grows on the north side of trees is unreliable and should not be trusted for navigation. Moss grows wherever conditions are damp and shaded, which depends on local terrain, moisture, and tree shape as much as on direction. While the shadier side of an isolated tree may hold more moss, using moss alone to find north can easily mislead you into travelling the wrong way.

title: Prevailing wind on trees
text: In exposed places where a steady prevailing wind blows, trees and shrubs may grow lopsided, with branches swept and more growth on the sheltered downwind side. If you know the usual wind direction for the area, this flagging can hint at orientation. It is a supporting clue rather than a precise method, since local terrain funnels wind and individual trees vary, so cross-check it with other signs.

title: Snow and sun patterns
text: Patterns in snow and vegetation can hint at direction when you know the local geography. Snow often lingers longer on shaded slopes that receive less sun, which in the Northern Hemisphere tend to face north, and melts faster on sunnier slopes facing south. In the Southern Hemisphere the sunnier aspect faces north. These clues depend on local terrain and weather and are best used to confirm, not replace, other methods.

title: Sun-side vegetation clues
text: Plants often grow more lushly on the side that receives more sunlight, which in the Northern Hemisphere is generally the southern side and in the Southern Hemisphere the northern side. Denser foliage, flowers, or ripening on one side of an isolated tree or clearing can hint at the sunny direction. Like other natural signs, these clues are influenced by local shade and moisture, so treat them as approximate.

title: Handrails in navigation
text: A handrail is a long, obvious linear feature such as a river, ridge, trail, fence, or coastline that you can follow to guide your travel in roughly the right direction. Keeping a handrail alongside you lets you move confidently without constantly checking a bearing, because the feature itself keeps you on line. Choosing a good handrail simplifies navigation and reduces the chance of drifting off course.

title: Catching features
text: A catching feature, or backstop, is a prominent landmark beyond your destination that tells you when you have gone too far, such as a river, road, or ridge lying past your target. If you reach the catching feature, you know to stop and turn back. Planning a catching feature into a route protects against overshooting an objective, especially in poor visibility when it is easy to walk past a small target.

title: Maintaining a bearing
text: Maintaining a consistent direction of travel over rough ground is aided by picking out a distant landmark that lies on your intended line, walking to it, and then choosing another beyond it. This keeps you moving straight when a feature is not continuously visible, and it avoids the tendency to wander in circles. Regularly checking your line against fixed reference points helps you hold a steady course.

title: Aiming off deliberately
text: Aiming off means intentionally steering to one known side of a small target that sits on a handrail, so when you reach the handrail you know which way to turn. For example, to find a bridge on a river, aim deliberately upstream of it; on reaching the river you turn downstream with certainty. This removes the guesswork of not knowing whether the target lies left or right of where you arrive.

title: Avoiding walking in circles
text: Without external references, people tend to walk in circles because small asymmetries in stride and perception go uncorrected. To travel straight, fix on distant landmarks and line up successive ones, use the sun or stars for a steady reference, or send someone ahead to keep you aligned. On featureless terrain in fog or darkness, this tendency is stronger, so deliberate direction-keeping techniques matter most.

title: Sun arc through the day
text: Over the course of a day the sun traces an arc across the sky, rising in the east, climbing to its highest point around midday, and setting in the west. In the Northern Hemisphere this arc leans toward the south, and in the Southern Hemisphere toward the north. Watching where the sun sits relative to that daily arc gives a continuous, if approximate, sense of direction throughout daylight hours.

title: Star movement and direction
text: Stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west as the Earth turns, except those near the celestial poles. By watching a star over several minutes against a fixed foreground marker, you can tell which way it is moving: a star rising is roughly east, setting is roughly west, climbing to the right suggests south, and falling to the right suggests north in the Northern Hemisphere. It is approximate.

title: Orion as a rough guide
text: The constellation Orion straddles the celestial equator and rises in the east and sets in the west from anywhere on Earth, making it a rough directional aid visible from both hemispheres in the appropriate season. The three stars of Orion's belt rise close to due east and set close to due west. Noting where Orion appears and how it moves offers another approximate east-west reference at night.

title: Cassiopeia and Polaris
text: The W or M shape of the constellation Cassiopeia lies on the opposite side of Polaris from the Big Dipper and circles the pole through the night. When the Big Dipper sits low or is hidden by terrain, Cassiopeia can help you locate Polaris, since the North Star lies roughly between the two. Using both constellations as backups makes finding true north more reliable across the changing night sky.

title: Judging distance by eye
text: Estimating distance without instruments relies on how clearly you can see detail: nearby objects show fine texture, while distant ones appear hazy, bluish, and simplified. Bright light, clear air, and looking across water or snow make things seem closer, while haze, dusk, and looking uphill make them seem farther. Cross-check estimates against known feature sizes, and expect error, especially over long ranges.

title: Reading the landscape ahead
text: Observing the shape of the land helps you anticipate terrain and route without instruments. Rivers flow downhill and often lead toward larger valleys and settlements, ridgelines offer views and drier travel, and vegetation changes hint at water and slope. Studying the landscape ahead lets you choose sensible lines of travel and recognise features, complementing any directional cues from the sun and stars.

title: Using shadows through the day
text: The direction and length of shadows change predictably through the day and give directional and timing cues. Shadows are long and point generally westward in the morning, shorten toward midday when they point along the north-south line, and lengthen pointing generally eastward in the afternoon. Watching how shadows swing and shrink offers a rough, continuous read of direction and the passage of time.

title: Estimating time until sunset
text: You can roughly estimate the time remaining until sunset by holding your hand at arm's length with fingers stacked horizontally between the sun and the horizon. Each finger width corresponds to very approximately fifteen minutes of remaining daylight, though this varies with latitude and season. It is a quick, tool-free way to judge whether you have time to reach a destination or must prepare to stop and shelter.

title: Following watercourses downhill
text: Water flows downhill, so following a stream or drainage generally leads to larger valleys, rivers, and often toward human habitation and easier travel. In many regions this is a traditional strategy for those who are lost, though it can also lead into gorges, cliffs, or dense terrain, and rivers may run away from help. Weigh the terrain and known geography before committing to following water blindly.

title: Recognising when you are lost
text: Admitting early that you are unsure of your position is a key survival skill, because continuing to push on usually makes the situation worse. If landmarks stop matching your expectations, stop, stay calm, and think before moving. Retrace to your last known position if it is safe, take stock of what you know, and avoid wandering, which wastes energy and can carry you far from where searchers expect you.

title: Marking your trail
text: In unfamiliar terrain, marking your route with small, noticeable signs such as stacked stones, arranged sticks, or scuffs can help you retrace your steps or allow rescuers to follow you. Place markers where you can see the next from the last, and note their pattern so you can read them in reverse. Trail marking supports both self-recovery and being found, but should not damage the environment needlessly.

title: Prominent landmarks as anchors
text: Identifying one or two prominent, hard-to-mistake landmarks such as a distinctive peak, tower, or coastline gives you fixed anchors to relate your movements to. Keeping track of where these landmarks sit relative to you as you travel helps maintain your sense of direction and position. When smaller features are confusing, returning your attention to a major landmark can re-establish your bearings.

title: Parts of a compass
text: A baseplate compass has a clear rectangular base with a direction-of-travel arrow, a rotating bezel marked in degrees, and a magnetic needle whose red end points to magnetic north. Inside the bezel is an orienting arrow and a set of parallel orienting lines. Understanding these parts is the basis for taking bearings, orienting a map, and following a course accurately across the landscape.

title: Orienting a map to north
text: Orienting a map means turning it so its features line up with the ground. Place a compass on the map, rotate the map and compass together until the map's north lines match the compass needle pointing north, accounting for declination. Once oriented, the map's layout matches the terrain around you, making it far easier to identify hills, valleys, and landmarks and to relate them to your position and route.

title: Magnetic versus true north
text: True north points to the geographic North Pole, while magnetic north is the direction a compass needle points, toward the Earth's shifting magnetic pole. Maps are usually drawn to true or grid north, so a compass bearing differs from a map bearing by an angle called declination or variation. Ignoring this difference leads to steady errors, so navigators adjust for it when converting between map and compass.

title: Understanding declination
text: Declination is the angle between true north and magnetic north at your location, and it varies from place to place and slowly over time. Maps state the local declination and its direction, east or west. You apply it when converting between grid and magnetic bearings so your compass and map agree. Because declination changes with location and year, always use the current value for the area you are travelling in.

title: Taking a bearing from a map
text: To take a bearing from a map, place the compass edge along your intended line of travel from start to destination, with the direction-of-travel arrow pointing the way you want to go. Rotate the bezel until its orienting lines align with the map's north-south grid lines. Read the bearing at the index, then adjust for declination to get the magnetic bearing you will actually follow on the ground.

title: Following a bearing
text: To follow a bearing, hold the compass level in front of you with the direction-of-travel arrow pointing ahead, and turn your whole body until the magnetic needle sits within the orienting arrow, sometimes described as putting the red in the shed. The direction-of-travel arrow now points along your bearing. Pick a landmark on that line, walk to it, and repeat to stay on course over distance.

title: Resection to find position
text: Resection, or triangulation, fixes your position when you can see two or more known landmarks. Take a compass bearing to each identifiable landmark, convert to map bearings, and draw a line back from each landmark on the map along its bearing. Your position lies where the lines cross. Using three landmarks gives a small triangle that confirms accuracy. This lets you locate yourself without knowing your position beforehand.

title: Reading contour lines
text: Contour lines join points of equal elevation, and reading them reveals the shape of the land. Lines close together indicate steep ground, while widely spaced lines show gentle slopes. Closed loops mark hilltops or depressions, and V-shaped contours point upstream along valleys and streams. Interpreting contours lets you picture terrain from a flat map, plan routes around obstacles, and match the map to what you see.

title: Terrain association
text: Terrain association means navigating by continuously comparing the map with the shape of the land around you rather than relying solely on precise bearings. By matching hills, valleys, ridges, streams, and slopes on the map to features you can see, you keep track of where you are as you move. This skill builds confidence, catches mistakes early, and works well in visible terrain alongside compass techniques.

title: Grid references basics
text: Many maps carry a grid of numbered squares that lets you describe a location as a grid reference. Read the horizontal numbers first, moving right, then the vertical numbers, moving up, a rule often remembered as along the corridor and up the stairs. Adding further digits by estimating within a square pinpoints a spot more precisely. Grid references give a common language for sharing and recording positions.

title: Pacing for distance
text: Pacing estimates distance travelled by counting steps. Determine your pace count over a known distance such as one hundred metres, typically counting each time the same foot strikes the ground. On the move, count paces to judge how far you have gone, remembering that rough, steep, or soft ground shortens your stride. Combined with a bearing, pacing helps you know when you have reached a distance target.

title: Estimating distance and time
text: Distance and travel time can be estimated by combining map measurement with an expected pace. A common planning aid, sometimes called Naismith's rule, allows a set walking speed on the flat plus extra time for climbing height gained. Terrain, load, weather, and fatigue all slow progress, so build in a margin. Estimating both distance and time helps set realistic goals and recognise when you may be off course.

title: Staying found
text: Staying found means maintaining awareness of your position throughout a journey rather than trying to relocate yourself only after becoming lost. Note landmarks, track your progress on the map, check bearings and time at each leg, and confirm features as you pass them. Frequent small checks are far easier than recovering from disorientation, and they let you catch and correct errors before they compound.

title: Thumbing the map
text: Thumbing the map is a simple technique for staying oriented: hold the map folded to the area you are in and keep your thumb on your current position, moving it along as you travel. This makes it quick to glance down and confirm where you are without searching the whole sheet. Combined with orienting the map to north, thumbing keeps you continuously aware of your location and heading.

title: Handrails with map and compass
text: Combining a handrail with map and compass work simplifies navigation. Identify a linear feature on the map, such as a stream or trail, that runs toward your objective, then follow it on the ground while occasionally checking your bearing and progress. The handrail keeps you roughly on line, reducing the need for constant precise bearing-following and freeing attention for watching the terrain and landmarks.

title: Setting a safety bearing
text: A safety bearing, or escape bearing, is a rough compass direction that will always lead you toward a known safe feature such as a road or valley if you become disoriented or visibility fails. Note it before entering difficult terrain. If things go wrong, following the safety bearing brings you to your catching feature and a way out. It is a planned fallback, not a precise route, but it prevents dangerous wandering.

title: Checking progress by legs
text: Breaking a route into legs, each running between recognisable points, makes navigation manageable and reduces error. For each leg, note the bearing, the distance or expected time, and a catching feature beyond the target. On reaching the end of a leg, confirm your position before starting the next. This structured approach keeps small mistakes contained to a single leg rather than accumulating across the whole journey.

title: Compass care and interference
text: A compass needle can be deflected by nearby metal, electronics, magnets, and some rocks or vehicles, giving false readings. Take bearings away from such sources, keeping the compass clear of belt buckles, phones, knives, and steel. Store the compass away from magnets, protect it from damage, and check it against a known direction if you doubt it. Understanding these limits keeps compass work reliable.

title: Back bearing to check position
text: A back bearing is the reverse of your travel bearing, found by adding or subtracting one hundred and eighty degrees. Sighting a back bearing to a landmark you have passed lets you confirm you are still on your intended line. If the reverse bearing to the feature no longer matches, you have drifted off course. Back bearings are a simple, powerful check for staying on a straight route.

title: Map scale and measuring distance
text: A map's scale states how ground distance relates to map distance, such as one to twenty-five thousand meaning one centimetre on the map equals two hundred and fifty metres on the ground. Use the scale bar or the ratio to measure route distances, remembering to account for winding paths and climbs, which lengthen actual travel. Knowing the scale lets you translate map measurements into realistic distances.

title: Choosing a route on the map
text: Planning a route on the map means weighing distance against terrain, hazards, and navigability. A longer path along a valley or trail may be faster and safer than a direct line over steep, broken ground. Look for handrails, catching features, and clear checkpoints, avoid cliffs and river crossings where possible, and match the route to the group's ability, the weather, and the available daylight.

title: Setting the map by inspection
text: You can orient a map without a compass by matching visible features to it. Turn the map until a recognisable line feature such as a road, river, or ridge on the map aligns with the same feature on the ground and other landmarks fall into their correct relative places. This quick technique keeps the map correctly oriented while you travel and is a fast way to relate the map to the terrain.

title: Attack points
text: An attack point is a large, easily found feature near a smaller, harder-to-locate objective. Navigate confidently to the obvious attack point first, then make a short, careful final approach on a precise bearing and distance to the target. This breaks a difficult find into an easy leg followed by a short accurate one, greatly improving the chance of locating small features in poor visibility or complex ground.

title: Collecting features along a leg
text: Collecting features, or tick features, are landmarks you expect to pass in sequence along a leg, such as a stream crossing, a bend in a trail, or a knoll. Ticking them off as you reach them confirms you are on track and shows your progress. If an expected feature fails to appear, it is an early sign that something is wrong, prompting you to stop and reassess before going further astray.

title: Contour features and shapes
text: Named contour shapes help you read and match terrain: a spur is a finger of higher ground extending outward, a re-entrant is a small valley or gully cutting inward, a saddle is a low point between two high points, and a knoll is a small hill. Recognising these shapes in the contour lines and on the ground lets you pinpoint your location and describe terrain precisely without relying only on bearings.

title: Steering around obstacles
text: When an obstacle such as a lake, crag, or dense thicket blocks a bearing, you can detour and regain your line by counting paces. Turn ninety degrees, count paces clear of the obstacle, resume your original bearing to pass it, then turn back and pace the same count to return to your original line before continuing. Careful counting keeps a detour from throwing you off your intended course.

title: Keeping the map dry and readable
text: In the field, protect the map from rain, wind, and wear by using a waterproof case or cover, and fold it to show the area in use. A damaged or soaked map is hard to read and may tear at creases just when you need it. Keeping the map accessible, dry, and folded to the current area supports frequent checking, which is the habit that keeps you found rather than lost.

title: Map symbols and legend
text: Maps use standardised symbols and colours to show roads, trails, buildings, water, vegetation, and terrain, all explained in the legend or key. Before relying on a map, study its legend so you can correctly interpret what the markings mean, since conventions vary between map series and countries. Understanding the symbols lets you read the map accurately and avoid mistaking one type of feature for another.

title: Grid north and true north
text: Many topographic maps are drawn on a grid whose north, called grid north, differs slightly from true north, and both differ from magnetic north. The map margin usually shows the small angles between these three norths. For most fieldwork the grid-to-magnetic difference is what matters when converting bearings. Being aware of all three norths prevents confusion when applying the map's stated angles precisely.

title: Slope and route effort
text: Contour spacing reveals slope, which strongly affects effort and time. Climbing steep ground is slow and tiring, and steep descents can be hazardous and hard on the knees. When planning, prefer gentler gradients and gaining or losing height gradually where possible. Reading slope from the map lets you anticipate the physical demands of a route and choose lines that suit the group and conditions.

title: Confirming position at checkpoints
text: At planned checkpoints along a route, deliberately confirm your position by matching several features around you to the map before continuing. Checking that contours, water, and landmarks all agree gives confidence you are where you think you are. Treating each checkpoint as a chance to catch errors, rather than assuming you are on track, keeps small navigational mistakes from growing into serious ones.

title: Practising navigation skills
text: Map and compass skills are perishable and best learned and practised in easy, low-risk conditions before you must rely on them in difficult terrain, poor weather, or an emergency. Regular practice builds the speed and confidence to orient a map, take and follow bearings, and read terrain under stress. Carrying a map and compass is only useful if you have practised the skills to use them well.

title: Not relying solely on electronics
text: Electronic navigation devices are useful but can fail through flat batteries, cold, damage, water, or loss of signal, so they should not be your only means of navigation in the wilderness. Carry a map and compass as a reliable backup and know how to use them. Treating a device as one tool among several, rather than the sole source of position, guards against being stranded when the electronics stop working.

title: Cumulus clouds
text: Cumulus are the puffy, cotton-like clouds with flat bases and rounded tops seen on fair days. Small, well-separated cumulus that stay flat usually indicate settled, pleasant weather. If they begin to grow tall and pile upward through the afternoon, they can develop into towering clouds capable of showers or thunderstorms, so watch for vertical growth as a sign of changing conditions.

title: Cumulonimbus thunderstorm clouds
text: Cumulonimbus are towering clouds that rise high into the atmosphere, often with a flattened, anvil-shaped top. They produce heavy rain, hail, strong gusts, and lightning. Seeing a rapidly building, dark, tall cloud is a warning to seek safe shelter before the storm arrives. Avoid exposed high ground and open water, and monitor for lightning and sudden wind shifts.

title: Stratus cloud layer
text: Stratus is a low, uniform, grey cloud layer that often covers the whole sky like a blanket. It can bring overcast skies, light drizzle, or mist, but usually not heavy rain. Stratus frequently forms in stable, moist air and may lift or thin as the day warms. It commonly reduces visibility, which matters for navigation in hilly or forested terrain.

title: Nimbostratus rain clouds
text: Nimbostratus is a thick, dark, featureless grey cloud layer that brings steady, prolonged rain or snow. Unlike brief showers from towering clouds, nimbostratus precipitation tends to be continuous and widespread, often lasting hours. Its arrival, especially after clouds thicken and lower, signals a period of persistent wet weather and reduced visibility.

title: Cirrus high clouds
text: Cirrus are thin, wispy, high-altitude clouds made of ice crystals, often appearing as delicate streaks or mares' tails. On their own they do not bring rain, but increasing and thickening cirrus can be an early sign that a weather front and unsettled conditions are approaching within a day or so. Treat spreading cirrus as a cue to watch the sky closely.

title: Altocumulus clouds
text: Altocumulus are mid-level clouds appearing as patches or rolls of white and grey, sometimes described as a mackerel sky. On a warm, humid morning, widespread altocumulus can indicate the atmosphere is becoming unstable and that thunderstorms may develop later in the day. They are a useful hint to plan activities earlier and monitor for building storm clouds.

title: Lenticular mountain clouds
text: Lenticular clouds are smooth, lens- or saucer-shaped clouds that form over and downwind of mountains where moist air flows across the peaks. They indicate strong winds aloft and turbulent air near the ridges. Their presence often warns of windy, unsettled mountain weather and can precede a change, so mountain travellers should treat them as a signal to stay cautious.

title: Lowering thickening clouds
text: When clouds progressively lower and thicken, the sky often changes from high thin cirrus to mid-level layers and finally to a low grey overcast. This sequence typically marks an approaching warm front and the onset of steady rain. Observing clouds descend and darken over several hours is one of the more reliable natural signs that wet weather is on the way.

title: Red sky saying
text: The old saying about a red sky at night pleasing sailors and a red sky in the morning warning them reflects that reddish evening skies can suggest dry air to the west, while red mornings can hint at approaching moisture. It is only a rough guide, tied to weather moving west to east in many regions, and should never replace careful observation of clouds, wind, and pressure.

title: Halo around sun
text: A ring or halo around the sun or moon is caused by light passing through ice crystals in high cirrostratus cloud. Because such high cloud often precedes a warm front, a halo can suggest that moisture is increasing and rain may follow within a day. It is a helpful early hint rather than a certainty, so combine it with other signs before deciding.

title: Wind shifts meaning
text: A noticeable shift in wind direction often marks the passage of a weather front. Winds backing or veering, together with changes in cloud and temperature, can signal that conditions are about to change. In many mid-latitude regions a swing toward the west or northwest after a front brings clearing, colder air, while a shift from the south can precede warmer, wetter weather.

title: Rising falling pressure
text: Atmospheric pressure trends are a strong weather clue. Steady or rising pressure generally indicates settling, fair conditions, while a marked fall often precedes wind, cloud, and rain. A rapid drop can warn of an approaching storm. Even without a barometer, you can infer trends from cloud sequences, wind changes, and how you feel, though instruments give clearer readings.

title: Dew and frost
text: Heavy dew or a frost on clear, calm mornings usually indicates that skies were cloudless overnight, allowing the ground to cool freely. This often accompanies stable, high-pressure conditions and suggests a continuing fair day. A morning with no dew under a cloudy sky can mean cloud has moved in overnight, which may hint at an approaching change in the weather.

title: Fast mountain weather
text: Weather in mountains can change quickly and dramatically, with clear skies giving way to cloud, wind, rain, or snow within a short time. Rising terrain forces air upward, cooling it and forming cloud and precipitation. Temperatures drop with altitude, and exposure increases. Always prepare for sudden deterioration, carry extra insulation, and be ready to turn back if conditions worsen.

title: Afternoon mountain thunderstorms
text: In many mountain regions, thunderstorms build in the afternoon as daytime heating lifts moist air over the peaks. Starting activities early and aiming to be off exposed summits and ridges by early afternoon reduces the risk of being caught by lightning, hail, and sudden downpours. Watch for cumulus clouds growing taller through the morning as an advance warning.

title: Lightning ridge danger
text: During a thunderstorm, avoid exposed ridges, summits, lone trees, and open water, as these locations raise the risk of a lightning strike. Move to lower ground and away from isolated tall objects. Seek shelter in a substantial building or a vehicle if possible. Do not shelter under a single tree in the open, and stay clear of metal objects and fences.

title: Lightning crouch position
text: If a thunderstorm catches you in the open with no shelter, minimise contact with the ground and your height. Crouch low on the balls of your feet with feet together, keeping your head down and hands off the ground. This is a last resort that offers only limited protection; the priority is always to reach a safe building or vehicle before the storm arrives.

title: Thirty thirty rule
text: The 30/30 lightning guideline suggests that if the time between seeing a lightning flash and hearing its thunder is 30 seconds or less, the storm is close enough to be dangerous and you should already be sheltering. Wait at least 30 minutes after the last thunder before leaving shelter, since strikes can occur even when a storm appears to have moved away.

title: Fog formation
text: Fog forms when air near the ground cools to its dew point and water vapour condenses into tiny droplets. It is common on clear, calm nights, in valleys where cold air pools, and near water. Fog sharply reduces visibility and can complicate navigation and travel. It often clears as the sun warms the ground, but in valleys and cold conditions it can persist for hours.

title: Signs of improving weather
text: Signs that weather is improving include rising pressure, clouds breaking up and lifting, cirrus and low cloud thinning, and a shift to drier, often cooler winds after a front passes. Clearing skies in the evening, decreasing wind, and the return of small fair-weather cumulus can all suggest settling conditions, though it is wise to confirm with several signs before relying on them.

title: Wind direction and fronts
text: Wind direction offers clues about approaching weather because winds tend to shift as fronts pass. In many mid-latitude areas, winds from a warmer, moister quarter can bring cloud and rain, while a change to a colder, drier quarter behind a front often brings clearer skies. Noting how the wind changes over hours, alongside cloud trends, helps you anticipate what is coming.

title: Spotting approaching storm
text: An approaching storm often announces itself with a darkening sky, tall building clouds, a distinct line of cloud on the horizon, gusty and shifting winds, a drop in temperature, and distant thunder or lightning. Recognising these signs early gives time to seek shelter and secure equipment. Treat a fast-moving dark cloud line and rising wind as a strong cue to prepare immediately.

title: Temperature drop before storms
text: A sudden drop in temperature and a gust of cooler wind often precede a thunderstorm or the passage of a cold front. This cool outflow, sometimes called a gust front, spreads ahead of the storm as rain-cooled air descends. Feeling the air turn noticeably cooler and windier under a darkening sky is a practical warning to move to shelter without delay.

title: Mares tails warning
text: Wispy cirrus clouds with hooked, trailing shapes are sometimes called mares' tails. When these high clouds increase and are followed by a lowering, thickening sheet of cloud, they can mark the leading edge of an approaching front and unsettled weather. On their own they are harmless, but a steady progression from mares' tails to overcast is a recognised sign of coming change.

title: Cloud cover overnight
text: Whether the sky is clear or cloudy overnight strongly affects temperature. Clear skies let heat radiate away, producing colder nights, dew, and frost, and often accompany stable fair weather. A cloudy night traps warmth, keeping temperatures higher, and can indicate that moisture and a possible change have moved in. Noting the night sky helps you anticipate the following day.

title: Wind and shelter
text: Wind direction and strength influence where to make camp and how weather will affect you. Sheltering on the leeward side of terrain, away from the prevailing wind, reduces chill and exposure. Rising, gusty winds can signal approaching weather, while a steady, moderate breeze from a fair quarter often accompanies settled conditions. Always secure gear when winds increase.

title: Severe bleeding pressure
text: For severe bleeding, apply firm, direct pressure over the wound using a clean pad, dressing, or your hand, and maintain it steadily. Pressure is the single most important step to control blood loss. If you can, help the injured person lie down. Call emergency services and get professional medical help as soon as possible, and keep applying pressure until help arrives.

title: Elevate bleeding limb
text: When practical and there is no suspected fracture, raising a bleeding arm or leg above the level of the heart while maintaining firm direct pressure can help reduce blood flow to the wound. Combine elevation with steady pressure rather than relying on it alone. Continue to monitor the casualty and seek professional medical help and emergency services for serious bleeding.

title: Pressure dressing application
text: To control bleeding once initial pressure has slowed it, apply a firm pressure dressing: place a clean pad over the wound and bind it snugly with a bandage to maintain pressure, but not so tight that it cuts off circulation beyond the dressing. Check that fingers or toes stay warm and pink. Seek professional medical help, and call emergency services for serious wounds.

title: Bleeding do not remove
text: If a dressing becomes soaked with blood, do not remove it, as this can disturb any clot that is forming. Instead, add a further dressing or pad on top and continue firm pressure. Removing the original dressing may restart heavy bleeding. Keep pressure maintained, reassure the casualty, and get urgent professional medical help by calling emergency services for severe bleeding.

title: Tourniquet last resort
text: A tourniquet should be used only for life-threatening bleeding from a limb that cannot be controlled by firm direct pressure, and it is a last resort. Apply it above the wound, tighten until bleeding stops, and clearly note the time it was applied. Do not loosen it once in place. This is a serious intervention; get emergency medical help urgently, as improper use carries risks.

title: Embedded object bleeding
text: If an object is embedded in a wound, do not remove it, because it may be limiting bleeding and removing it can cause more damage. Instead, apply pressure around the object rather than directly on it, and build up padding on either side to support it before bandaging. Keep the casualty still and seek urgent professional medical help by calling emergency services.

title: Cleaning a wound
text: For a minor wound, first control any bleeding, then clean it by rinsing with clean, safe water to flush out dirt and debris. Gently remove visible grit if you can do so easily. Avoid scrubbing deep wounds. Pat the surrounding skin dry and cover with a clean dressing. For deep, dirty, or large wounds, or if you cannot clean them, seek professional medical help.

title: Covering a wound
text: After cleaning a wound, cover it with a sterile or clean, non-stick dressing to keep it protected and reduce contamination. Change the dressing if it becomes wet or dirty, using clean hands. A covered wound is less likely to be irritated and can heal more comfortably. Watch for signs of infection over the following days and seek medical help if they appear.

title: Wound infection signs
text: Signs that a wound may be infected include increasing redness, swelling, warmth, pain, pus or discharge, a bad smell, red streaks spreading from the wound, and fever or feeling generally unwell. Infection can become serious if untreated. If you notice these signs, seek professional medical help promptly, and treat spreading redness, streaks, or fever as reasons to get urgent care.

title: When to seek wound care
text: Seek professional medical help for wounds that are deep, gaping, or long; that will not stop bleeding; that are heavily contaminated; that involve the face, joints, hands, or genitals; that are caused by animal or human bites; or that show signs of infection. Puncture wounds and those with embedded material also need assessment. When in doubt, get the wound checked by a professional.

title: Tetanus consideration
text: Wounds, especially those that are deep, dirty, or caused by punctures, bites, or contact with soil, can carry a risk of tetanus. Anyone with such a wound should seek professional medical advice about whether they need a tetanus vaccination or booster, particularly if their immunisation is out of date or unknown. Cleaning the wound thoroughly is important, but it does not remove the need for advice.

title: Cooling a burn
text: For a burn, cool the affected area as soon as possible with cool or lukewarm running water for about 20 minutes. Do not use ice, iced water, or very cold sources, as these can worsen the injury. Cooling helps limit damage and eases pain. After cooling, cover the burn loosely, keep the person warm overall, and seek medical help for anything but a small, minor burn.

title: Remove items from burn
text: When treating a burn, gently remove jewellery, watches, belts, and any tight or restrictive clothing from the affected area before it begins to swell, as long as these are not stuck to the skin. Do not try to peel away clothing that is stuck to the burn. Removing loose constricting items early helps prevent problems from swelling. Seek medical help for significant burns.

title: Covering a burn
text: After cooling a burn, cover it loosely with a clean, non-stick dressing or a layer of clean cling film to protect it and reduce the risk of infection. Do not wrap tightly. Cling film should be laid over the burn rather than wound around a limb. Keep the casualty warm, monitor them, and seek professional medical help for burns that are large, deep, or otherwise concerning.

title: Do not pop blisters
text: Do not deliberately burst or pop blisters that form on a burn, because intact blisters help protect the underlying skin and reduce infection risk. Cover the area gently with a clean, non-stick dressing. If a large or troublesome blister develops, have it assessed by a medical professional rather than opening it yourself. Keep the area clean and watch for signs of infection.

title: No butter on burns
text: Do not apply butter, oils, toothpaste, ointments, or creams to a burn, as these can trap heat, increase the risk of infection, and interfere with later medical care. The correct immediate treatment is cooling with running water and then a clean, loose, non-stick covering. Avoid home remedies. For burns that are large, deep, or on sensitive areas, seek professional medical help.

title: Burns needing medical care
text: Seek urgent medical help for burns that are large or deep; that involve the face, hands, feet, joints, or genitals; that go all the way around a limb; or that are caused by electricity or chemicals. Also get help for burns in children, older people, or anyone unwell, and for any burn you are unsure about. Call emergency services for serious or extensive burns.

title: Chemical and electrical burns
text: Chemical and electrical burns need special caution. For chemicals, protect yourself, remove contaminated clothing, and rinse the area with plenty of clean water for a prolonged period. For electrical injuries, ensure the power source is off and it is safe before approaching. Both types can be more serious than they look, so always seek professional medical help and call emergency services.

title: Signs of a fracture
text: Signs that a bone may be broken include pain that worsens with movement, swelling, bruising, deformity or an unnatural position, difficulty using the limb, and sometimes a grating sensation. You may not always be able to tell a fracture from a bad sprain. When in doubt, treat it as a fracture, keep it still, and seek professional medical help.

title: Immobilise a fracture
text: The main aim in treating a suspected fracture is to keep the injured part still, as movement causes pain and can worsen the injury. Support the limb in the position found, using padding, and avoid unnecessary movement. Do not attempt to test whether the bone is broken by moving it. Keep the casualty still and comfortable, and arrange professional medical help.

title: Splinting a limb
text: A splint supports and immobilises a suspected fracture using a rigid object padded against the limb. Where possible, secure it so that it holds the joints both above and below the injury still, which prevents movement at the break. Ties should be snug but not so tight that they cut off circulation. Splinting is a temporary measure before reaching professional medical care.

title: Pad the splint
text: When applying a splint, place soft padding between the rigid support and the limb, and around bony areas, to improve comfort and reduce pressure. A well-padded splint is less likely to cause further harm. Secure it firmly enough to prevent movement but check that it is not so tight that circulation is impaired. Seek professional medical help once the limb is supported.

title: Check circulation past splint
text: After applying a splint or firm bandage, regularly check circulation beyond it by looking at the fingers or toes: they should stay warm, and their colour should return quickly after gentle pressure. Numbness, tingling, coldness, or a bluish colour suggests the splint is too tight and must be loosened. Ongoing monitoring is important while awaiting professional medical help.

title: Do not straighten deformity
text: In general, do not attempt to straighten or realign a severely deformed limb or a suspected fracture, as this can cause further injury. Support and immobilise it in the position found, with padding, and keep the casualty still. Correcting deformities is a task for trained medical professionals. Arrange urgent medical help, and call emergency services for serious injuries.

title: Open fracture care
text: An open fracture, where the skin is broken and bone may be visible, carries a high risk of infection and bleeding. Control bleeding with pressure around the wound rather than directly on protruding bone, and cover the wound with a clean dressing. Immobilise the limb and do not push bone back in. This is a serious injury needing urgent professional medical help.

title: RICE for sprains
text: For a sprain or strain, the RICE approach can help in the early stages: Rest the injured part, apply Ice or a cold pack wrapped in cloth, use gentle Compression with a bandage, and Elevate the limb. This aims to reduce pain and swelling. Avoid putting weight on a painful injury, and seek professional medical help if it is severe or does not improve.

title: Avoid heat early
text: In the first day or two after a sprain or strain, avoid applying heat, hot baths, or heat rubs to the injured area, as heat can increase swelling and bleeding in the tissues early on. Cold packs, rest, gentle compression, and elevation are more appropriate at this stage. If pain or swelling is severe or persists, seek professional medical advice.

title: Sprain when to seek help
text: Seek professional medical help for a sprain or strain if you cannot bear weight or use the limb, if there is severe pain, marked swelling, deformity, numbness, or if the injury does not improve over a few days. These signs may indicate a fracture or a more serious injury. When you are unsure whether an injury is a sprain or a break, have it assessed.

title: Causes of shock
text: Shock is a life-threatening condition in which the circulation fails to deliver enough blood to the body's tissues. Common causes include severe bleeding, serious burns, major injury, severe fluid loss, and serious infection or allergic reactions. Recognising shock early and treating the underlying cause are vital. Always call emergency services, as shock requires urgent professional medical help.

title: Signs of shock
text: Signs of shock can include pale, cold, clammy skin; sweating; a rapid, weak pulse; rapid, shallow breathing; nausea; thirst; weakness; restlessness; and later confusion, drowsiness, or loss of consciousness. These indicate the body is struggling to maintain circulation. If you suspect shock, treat it as an emergency, call for help, and get urgent professional medical care.

title: Treating shock position
text: If someone shows signs of shock, help them lie down and, if there is no injury preventing it, raise their legs to improve blood flow to vital organs. Keep them warm with a blanket or coat, loosen tight clothing, and reassure them calmly. Treat any obvious cause, such as bleeding. Call emergency services urgently, as shock needs professional medical care.

title: Shock no food drink
text: A person in shock should not be given anything to eat or drink, even if they say they are thirsty, because they may need surgery and because their condition can deteriorate. You may moisten their lips if they are dry. Keep them lying down, warm, and reassured while you treat the cause and wait for help. Call emergency services and get urgent medical care.

title: Recognising hypothermia
text: Hypothermia occurs when the body loses heat faster than it can produce it and core temperature falls. Early signs include shivering, cold and pale skin, tiredness, and clumsiness. As it worsens, shivering may stop, and confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness, and slowed breathing appear. Severe hypothermia is life-threatening. Get the person warm and seek urgent professional medical help.

title: Remove wet clothing
text: For someone with hypothermia, one of the most important steps is to get them out of the cold and wind and to replace wet clothing with dry, warm layers, since wet clothes draw heat away rapidly. Handle them gently and shelter them from the elements. Insulate them from the cold ground as well. Seek professional medical help, especially for severe cases.

title: Insulate against cold
text: To help a hypothermic person, insulate them from cold, wind, and the ground using dry clothing, blankets, a sleeping bag, or other materials, covering the head as well since heat is lost there. Trapping warmth around the body allows gradual rewarming. Avoid direct intense heat. Continue to monitor them and arrange professional medical help, calling emergency services for severe cases.

title: Warm gradually not rubbing
text: Rewarm a hypothermic person gradually and gently. Do not rub their limbs or skin and do not use direct intense heat such as a fire held close, hot water bottles against bare skin, or immersion in hot water, as sudden rewarming and rough handling can be dangerous. Shelter, dry insulation, and warm surroundings are safer. Seek professional medical help promptly.

title: Warm drinks if alert
text: A person with mild hypothermia who is fully conscious and able to swallow safely may be given warm, sweet, non-alcoholic drinks to help provide comfort and energy. Never give drinks to someone who is drowsy, confused, or not fully alert, because of the risk of choking. Avoid alcohol, which increases heat loss. Seek professional medical help for anything beyond mild cases.

title: Handle hypothermia gently
text: Handle a severely hypothermic person very gently and keep them as still as possible, because rough movement can be harmful when the body is very cold. Avoid unnecessary jostling, keep them horizontal, and continue to insulate and shelter them while awaiting help. Severe hypothermia is a medical emergency, so call emergency services and get urgent professional medical care.

title: Signs of frostbite
text: Frostbite is freezing of the skin and deeper tissues, most often affecting fingers, toes, ears, nose, and cheeks. Early signs include cold, numb skin that may look pale or waxy, with pins and needles. As it deepens, the area becomes hard, and the skin may turn white, grey, or blistered. Frostbite needs prompt, careful treatment and professional medical help.

title: Do not rub frostbite
text: Do not rub or massage frostbitten skin, and do not apply direct high heat such as a fire, stove, or hot water, because rubbing and intense heat can cause further tissue damage to the numb, fragile area. Instead, protect the part from further cold and handle it gently. Get the person to warmth and seek professional medical help for proper rewarming and care.

title: Rewarm frostbite carefully
text: Frostbitten areas should be rewarmed gradually, ideally in warm, not hot, water, but only when there is no risk that the part will freeze again, since refreezing thawed tissue is very harmful. Rewarming can be painful. If refreezing is possible or medical care is near, it is often safer to keep the part protected and seek professional help promptly.

title: Do not walk on frostbite
text: If someone's feet are frostbitten, avoid having them walk on the affected feet whenever possible, as this can worsen the injury, unless walking is unavoidable to reach safety. Keep the feet protected and, once rewarmed, prevent refreezing. Frostbite requires assessment and treatment by a medical professional, so arrange to get the person to proper medical care.

title: Heatstroke emergency
text: Heatstroke is a life-threatening emergency in which the body overheats and can no longer regulate its temperature. Signs may include very hot skin, confusion, agitation, rapid breathing and pulse, headache, and loss of consciousness. Call emergency services immediately, move the person to shade or a cool place, and begin cooling them urgently while awaiting professional medical help.

title: Cooling for heatstroke
text: While waiting for emergency help for suspected heatstroke, cool the person aggressively: move them to shade, remove excess clothing, and cool the skin with water, wet cloths, fanning, or cold packs at the neck, armpits, and groin. Rapid cooling is critical. Do not delay calling emergency services, as heatstroke can be fatal and always requires urgent professional medical care.

title: Heat exhaustion treatment
text: Heat exhaustion, a milder condition than heatstroke, may cause heavy sweating, tiredness, dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps, and a fast, weak pulse. Move the person to a cool, shaded place, have them rest, loosen clothing, cool the skin, and give sips of water if they are alert. If they do not improve within about half an hour or worsen, seek urgent medical help.

title: Rehydrate with sips
text: To treat mild dehydration, drink safe fluids steadily, taking small, frequent sips rather than large amounts at once, especially if the person feels nauseous. Rest in a cool place and continue drinking until urine lightens and symptoms ease. If vomiting prevents fluid intake, or if severe symptoms appear, seek professional medical help, as intravenous fluids may be needed.

title: Oral rehydration solution
text: Oral rehydration solutions, which contain balanced amounts of salts and sugar in water, help the body absorb fluid and replace losses from sweating, vomiting, or diarrhoea. Commercial sachets are ideal where available. Drink the solution in small, frequent sips. If dehydration is severe, or the person cannot keep fluids down or becomes confused, seek urgent professional medical help.

title: Severe dehydration help
text: Severe dehydration is dangerous and may cause confusion, a rapid weak pulse, very little or no urine, sunken eyes, extreme weakness, or loss of consciousness. It can be life-threatening and may require medical fluids. If someone shows these signs, or cannot keep fluids down, seek urgent professional medical help and call emergency services rather than relying on drinking alone.

title: Adult choking back blows
text: If an adult is choking and cannot cough, speak, or breathe, encourage any effective coughing first. If coughing fails, lean them forward and give up to five sharp back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand, checking after each to see if the blockage has cleared. If back blows do not work, move on to abdominal thrusts, and call emergency services.

title: Adult abdominal thrusts
text: If back blows do not relieve choking in a responsive adult, give abdominal thrusts: stand behind them, place a fist just above the navel, grasp it with your other hand, and pull sharply inward and upward up to five times. Alternate five back blows and five abdominal thrusts, and call emergency services. Anyone who has received abdominal thrusts should be medically checked.

title: Infant choking differences
text: A choking infant is treated differently from an adult. Support the baby face down along your forearm with the head low and give up to five back blows between the shoulder blades. Then turn the baby face up and give up to five chest thrusts using two fingers on the breastbone. Do not give abdominal thrusts to an infant. Call emergency services urgently.

title: Choking becomes unconscious
text: If a choking person becomes unconscious, call emergency services immediately if not already done, lower them safely to the ground, and begin CPR if you are trained, checking the mouth for any visible obstruction before giving breaths. Do not perform blind finger sweeps. Continue resuscitation efforts until help arrives. Formal first-aid training greatly improves the ability to respond.

title: Check responsiveness breathing
text: If someone collapses, check whether they respond by talking to them and gently shaking their shoulders, then check whether they are breathing normally by looking at the chest and listening for a short time. If they are unresponsive and not breathing normally, treat it as a cardiac arrest, call emergency services immediately, and begin CPR if you are trained to do so.

title: Call for help first
text: In a suspected cardiac arrest, calling emergency services quickly is critical, so summon help or ask a bystander to call while you start CPR. Early professional help and defibrillation greatly improve survival. If you are alone with an adult and have a phone, call first, then begin chest compressions. Report the location clearly and follow any instructions the dispatcher gives you.

title: Chest compressions basics
text: Chest compressions maintain some blood flow during cardiac arrest. For an adult, place the heel of one hand in the centre of the chest with the other on top, keep your arms straight, and press down firmly and regularly, allowing the chest to recoil fully between compressions. Guidance is generally around 100 to 120 compressions a minute. Formal training is strongly recommended.

title: Hands only CPR
text: Hands-only CPR, meaning continuous chest compressions without rescue breaths, is a simple approach that untrained or unconfident bystanders can use for an adult in cardiac arrest until help arrives. Push hard and fast in the centre of the chest and do not stop unnecessarily. It can save lives, but completing a recognised first-aid course provides fuller skills and confidence.

title: AED use
text: An automated external defibrillator, or AED, is a device that analyses the heart rhythm and can deliver a shock to help restart an effective heartbeat. If one is available during a cardiac arrest, send someone to fetch it, switch it on, and follow its clear spoken instructions while continuing compressions between prompts. AEDs are designed for public use, but training builds confidence.

title: CPR training recommended
text: The guidance here on CPR is general and is not a substitute for hands-on instruction. Attending a recognised first-aid or CPR course teaches correct technique, depth, rate, and rescue breaths, and builds the confidence to act in an emergency. If you may need to respond to collapses in remote settings, formal training is strongly recommended before it is ever needed.

title: Remove bee sting
text: If a bee sting leaves the sting in the skin, remove it as quickly as possible by scraping it out sideways with a fingernail or a firm edge, rather than pinching it, which may squeeze in more venom. Then clean the area and apply a cold compress to ease pain and swelling. Watch for any signs of a severe allergic reaction and seek help if they appear.

title: Insect sting care
text: For most insect stings, clean the area, apply a cold compress or cold pack wrapped in cloth to reduce pain and swelling, and keep the affected part still and slightly raised if possible. Avoid scratching. Simple pain relief may help. Watch carefully for signs of a spreading or severe allergic reaction, and seek urgent medical help if breathing or swelling worsens.

title: Allergic reaction from sting
text: After an insect bite or sting, watch for signs of a serious allergic reaction, such as widespread rash, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, difficulty breathing, wheezing, dizziness, or collapse. These are a medical emergency. Call emergency services immediately, and if the person has a prescribed adrenaline auto-injector, help them use it without delay.

title: Tick removal
text: To remove a tick, use fine-tipped tweezers or a tick removal tool to grasp it as close to the skin as possible, then pull upward with steady, even pressure without twisting or jerking, so the mouthparts are not left behind. Do not crush the tick's body. Clean the area afterward. Watch for a spreading rash or illness and seek medical advice if these occur.

title: Mosquito disease awareness
text: In some regions, mosquitoes can transmit diseases. Reducing bites by covering skin, using appropriate repellents, and sleeping under nets where advised lowers the risk. If you develop fever, chills, headache, or feel unwell after being in an area where mosquito-borne disease occurs, seek professional medical advice promptly and mention your recent travel and exposure to insects.

title: Snake bite stay calm
text: If someone is bitten by a snake, keep them calm and as still as possible, since movement can spread venom more quickly. Reassure them, move them away from the snake, and do not attempt to catch it. Note its appearance only if you can do so safely and from a distance. Get the person to medical care urgently, as antivenom may be needed.

title: Snake bite immobilise limb
text: After a snake bite, keep the bitten limb still and, in general, positioned at or below the level of the heart or immobilised to slow the spread of venom. Remove rings, watches, and tight clothing near the bite before swelling develops. Keep the person calm and get them to professional medical care as quickly and gently as possible, calling emergency services.

title: Snake bite do nots
text: For a snake bite, do not cut the wound, do not try to suck out venom, do not apply a tight tourniquet, and do not apply ice, as these traditional measures can cause harm and do not remove venom. Instead, keep the person still and calm, immobilise the limb, and get them to medical care urgently. Antivenom and professional treatment are what save lives.

title: Snake bite get help
text: A snake bite should always be treated as a potential emergency, even if it seems minor, because symptoms can develop later.
